c-hagia-sophia.group: Byzantine — the domes and the cistern
c-hagia-sophia.angle_note: the runes are in the upper gallery: one home

old_cards.name: Hagia Sophia
old_cards.teaser: The dome came down once already, and the one overhead is the replacement.
old_cards.body: Justinian's church was inaugurated on 27 December 537, built in five years and ten months by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. The first dome fell in the earthquake of 7 May 558; Isidore the Younger rebuilt it higher and steeper by 562, and that is the dome overhead. Cathedral for nine centuries, mosque from 1453, museum from 1935, mosque again since July 2020. Sultanahmet · the EUR 25 ticket covers the upper gallery; the ground floor is a working prayer hall and closes to visitors around the five daily prayers

old_cards.name: Halfdan's runes
old_cards.teaser: A Varangian guardsman got bored during a service and carved his name.
old_cards.body: In 1964 a runic inscription about twenty-three centimetres long was found scratched into the marble parapet of Hagia Sophia's upper south gallery. Only the ending, -ftan, is legible; runologists read it as Halfdan and reconstruct the ordinary Norse formula behind it — Halfdan carved these runes. He would have been one of the Varangians, the Norse and later Anglo-Saxon mercenaries who guarded Byzantine emperors from the late tenth century. A second name, Ári, surfaced in 1975. Upper south gallery — inside the ticketed visiting route, not the prayer floor

c-chora.group: Byzantine — the domes and the cistern

old_cards.name: Chora — Kariye Mosque
old_cards.teaser: The finest Byzantine mosaic cycle anywhere, and three panels of it are behind curtains.
old_cards.body: Theodore Metochites, Grand Logothete under Andronikos II, paid for the mosaics and frescoes between about 1315 and 1321 and had himself worked into the panel above the door, handing the church over to Christ. He later fell from power and died as a monk inside it. Converted to a mosque in the early sixteenth century, made a museum in 1945, returned to worship and reopened on 6 May 2024 after four years of restoration. The narthex cycles are all visible; the figural mosaics in the prayer hall are veiled. Edirnekapı, Fatih · daily 09:00-18:00; no visitor entry on Fridays or during the five daily prayers

c-cistern.group: Byzantine — the domes and the cistern

old_cards.name: Basilica Cistern
old_cards.teaser: Two Medusa heads used as furniture, one on her side, one upside down.
old_cards.body: Justinian's reservoir was built around 532 beneath a public basilica, which is where the name comes from. Three hundred and thirty-six columns, most of them scavenged from older buildings, carried water to the Great Palace above. In the north-west corner two carved Medusa heads serve as column bases, one laid sideways, one inverted, with no surviving explanation for either. It reopened in July 2022 after five years of restoration and seismic strengthening; management passed to the state foundations body in June 2026, which briefly closed it. Yerebatan Cad., Sultanahmet · daily 09:00-18:30, night visit 19:30-22:00 · cards and İstanbulkart only, no cash

c-suleymaniye.group: Ottoman — the mosque and the palace

old_cards.name: Süleymaniye Mosque
old_cards.teaser: Sinan piped the lamp smoke into one room and turned the soot into ink.
old_cards.body: Begun 1550, finished 1557, and never only a mosque: it came with four madrasas, a medical school, a hospital, a soup kitchen, a caravanserai and a hamam. Süleyman lies in the garden tomb, Hürrem Sultan in hers of 1558, and Sinan in a small tomb at the corner of the wall he built. Above the entrance he set a chamber that drew oil-lamp smoke off the walls; the collected soot went to the palace calligraphers. Süleymaniye, Fatih · free entry, closed to visitors around the five prayers · one of the four zones UNESCO inscribed as the Historic Areas of Istanbul in 1985

c-topkapi.group: Ottoman — the mosque and the palace
c-topkapi.angle_note: the imperial kitchens are inside Topkapı: one home

old_cards.name: Topkapı Palace
old_cards.teaser: The Quran is read aloud, all day, in the room that has held the relics since 1517.
old_cards.body: Mehmed II ordered construction from 1459; the palace was finished around 1478 and governed the empire until the court moved to Dolmabahçe in 1856. The Chamber of the Sacred Relics has held its collection since 1517, when Selim I took Cairo and the caliphate came north — and the practice of recitation came with it, kept now by a rota of readers through opening hours. In the Treasury: the Topkapı dagger and the eighty-six-carat Spoonmaker's Diamond. Sultanahmet · 09:00-17:30, closed Tuesdays · one combined ticket now covers the palace, the Harem and Hagia Irene

old_cards.name: Matbah-ı Âmire — the imperial kitchens
old_cards.teaser: Eight hundred cooks, four thousand fed daily — and the restraint you still taste.
old_cards.body: The Topkapı kitchens employed more than 800 people and cooked for roughly 4,000 a day. Fire took them in 1574 and Mimar Sinan rebuilt them: ten domed buildings, two rows of twenty wide chimneys. That scale bred a style — measured spicing, rice over bulgur, vegetables cooked in olive oil and eaten cold — which is still what Istanbul means when it calls a dish its own rather than Anatolia's. The rooms now hold 10,700 pieces of Chinese porcelain. WHERE Topkapı Palace, Sultanahmet · the kitchens run down one side of the second courtyard

old_cards.name: Istanbul Archaeological Museums
old_cards.teaser: The painter who dug up the Alexander Sarcophagus then built a museum around it.
old_cards.body: Osman Hamdi Bey excavated the royal necropolis at Sidon in 1887 and brought back a Pentelic marble sarcophagus with its painted surfaces still partly legible — Macedonian and Persian figures fighting in colour. The museum he founded around the find opened on 13 June 1891 and holds roughly a million objects, among them two of the three tablets of the Kadesh treaty of about 1259 BC, the oldest known peace treaty; the United Nations hangs a copy in New York. Osman Hamdi Bey Yokuşu, Gülhane, Fatih · entered from the first court of Topkapı or from Gülhane Park; ticketed separately from the palace

old_cards.name: Istanbul Modern
old_cards.teaser: A viewing terrace hovering over a sheet of water covering the whole roof.
old_cards.body: Founded in 2004 as Türkiye's first museum of modern and contemporary art, it started in a Karaköy warehouse, moved out in 2018, and returned to the same stretch of waterfront on 4 May 2023 in Renzo Piano's first building in the country. The aluminium facade is cut to catch the strait's light. On the roof a terrace stands above a shallow reflecting plane, so the water on the building and the water below run together. Semiha Berksoy's retrospective closes 6 September 2026. Tophane İskele Cad. 1/1, Beyoğlu (Galataport) · Tue-Thu and Sat-Sun 10:00-18:00, Fri to 20:00, closed Mondays

old_cards.name: Istanbul Modern
old_cards.teaser: Renzo Piano put a pool on the roof and the city behind it.
old_cards.body: Renzo Piano's building opened on 4 May 2023 inside Galataport, close to where the 1950s customs warehouse the museum used to occupy stood before it was pulled down — five storeys and 10,500 square metres holding exhibition halls, a cinema, a library, a design shop, a café and a restaurant, with a reflection pool five centimetres deep on the roof terrace facing the historic peninsula and the Galata Tower. Ticketed, which makes the roof an hour of looking rather than a desk. Go on a weekday morning, before the cruise ships unload onto the same quay. Galataport, Karaköy, Beyoğlu · ticketed entry

old_cards.name: Pera Museum
old_cards.teaser: An 1893 hotel that now owns the record-breaking Turkish painting.
old_cards.body: The building opened in 1893 as the Bristol, one of the Pera hotels that took Orient Express traffic alongside the Pera Palace and the Tokatlıyan. Its facade was kept and everything behind it rebuilt as galleries; the Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation opened the museum on 8 June 2005. The anchor is Osman Hamdi Bey's The Tortoise Trainer , painted in 1906 and bought at auction in December 2004 for a sum that was then a record for a Turkish work. Meşrutiyet Cad., Tepebaşı, Beyoğlu · Tue-Sat 10:00-19:00 (Fri to 22:00), Sun 12:00-18:00, closed Mondays · free Fridays 18:00-22:00, free for students on Wednesdays

c-cicek.angle_note: the building and what it tells; 'read, don't eat' is the advice. The 1942–64 story is told in the food-history fold: one clause

old_cards.name: Çiçek Pasajı
old_cards.teaser: Built on the ashes of the empire's opera house, named after Russian refugees.
old_cards.body: The Naum Theatre stood here — the Ottoman capital's chief opera house, staging Verdi, with Sultans Abdülaziz and Abdülhamid II in the audience — until the Pera fire of 1870. The Greek banker Hristaki Zoğrafos bought the ruin and had Kleanthis Zannos build the Cité de Péra on it in 1876: twenty-four shops below, eighteen apartments above. Destitute Russian noblewomen who arrived after 1917 sold flowers in the corridor, and by the 1940s the name had stuck. The building failed in 1978 and was rebuilt by 1988. The clientele was not. İstiklal Caddesi at Galatasaray, Beyoğlu · further restoration work in 2005 and 2022

old_cards.name: Çiçek Pasajı
old_cards.teaser: The prettiest arcade on İstiklal, and the clearest map of what was taken.
old_cards.body: Built in 1876 as the Cité de Péra by the Greek banker Hristaki Zoğrafos, on ground cleared by the 1870 Pera fire that destroyed the Naum Theatre — a Second Empire arcade of European shops and apartments. As Pera declined the shops became rough meyhanes: beer barrels rolled onto the pavement, marble slabs laid across them. It was restored in 1988, and again since. The building came back. The clientele did not. İstiklal Cad., Beyoğlu · walk it, then eat elsewhere

old_cards.name: Zeki Müren
old_cards.teaser: Turkey's most beloved voice belonged to its most flamboyant man, and nobody minded.
old_cards.body: Born in Bursa, schooled in Istanbul, he entered the State Academy of Fine Arts in 1950 and made his first live broadcast on Istanbul Radio on 1 January 1951. He then held the stage at the Maksim gazino in Taksim for eleven years — the big-room, orchestra-backed successor to the meyhane's fasıl nights. A sequinned jacket from 1958, a miniskirt from 1970, and no loss of affection from a conservative public. He collapsed and died at a TRT ceremony on 24 September 1996, leaving everything to two charitable foundations. Taksim · the Maksim gazino closed in 2005 and the site is now a hotel

old_cards.name: The Black Russian
old_cards.teaser: The man who brought jazz to Istanbul was born in Mississippi to freed slaves.
old_cards.body: Frederick Bruce Thomas was born in Coahoma County, Mississippi in November 1872 to parents who had been enslaved. He reached Moscow by way of London, ran theatres and restaurants there for nineteen years, and fled the revolution to Constantinople. By Vladimir Alexandrov's account he opened Stella in Şişli, then Maxim in Taksim in 1921, and the city heard the foxtrot, the Charleston and live jazz through him. Refused a United States passport and buried in debt, he died in a debtors' prison in June 1928. Şişli and Taksim · the Maksim name outlived him on Taksim until 2005 · biography: Vladimir Alexandrov, The Black Russian

old_cards.name: Yenikapı — the dig that held up the railway
old_cards.teaser: Digging the Bosphorus rail tunnel turned up a settlement 8,500 years old.
old_cards.body: Salvage excavation at Yenikapı ran from 2004 to 2013 and held the Marmaray project up for years. It exposed the Theodosian Harbour and thirty-seven shipwrecks of the fifth to eleventh centuries, the largest group of medieval ships ever found on a single site. Below the harbour floor came something much older: dwelling foundations, burials and human footprints from roughly 8,500 years ago, when the Sea of Marmara was still a lake. Sixty thousand objects in all. Yenikapı, Fatih — now a transport interchange · the finds are held by the Istanbul Archaeological Museums

old_cards.name: Tünel
old_cards.teaser: Twelve years after London, the second underground railway on earth — 573 metres.
old_cards.body: The French engineer Eugène-Henri Gavand built it to solve exactly one problem: the climb from the port at Galata to the merchant quarter at Pera. It opened on 17 January 1875, which makes it the second-oldest underground urban railway in the world after the London Underground of 1863. Five hundred and seventy-three metres of it, about sixty of them vertical. It ran on steam until the renovation that closed the line in 1968; electrified and reopened in 1971, it is still doing the only job it was built for. Karaköy to Tünel Meydanı, Beyoğlu · two stations, a ride of well under two minutes · İstanbulkart accepted

old_cards.name: Sultanahmet Meydanı — the Hippodrome
old_cards.teaser: You are standing on the racetrack — about 450 metres of it, under two metres of fill.
old_cards.body: Septimius Severus laid a hippodrome here around AD 203; Constantine rebuilt it in 324–330 as the centrepiece of his new capital — roughly 450 by 130 metres, stands for some 100,000 people. The long oval of today's square is the track itself, and the three monuments standing in their sunken pits mark the spina, the central barrier the chariots turned around: Thutmose III's granite obelisk (the guide's Curiosities section tells its story), the Serpent Column brought from Delphi where it celebrated the Greek victory over Persia at Plataea — the oldest Greek object in the city — and the Walled Obelisk, stripped of its gilded bronze by the Fourth Crusade in 1204. The pits exist because the modern ground sits about two metres above the ancient track. The Nika riots began here in 532 and burned half the city; the last recorded race ran in 1200. What the square is for: reading fifteen centuries in a single flat ten-minute walk, free, at any hour — the German Fountain of 1900, Kaiser Wilhelm II's gift, closes the north end. The tell — The Serpent Column, from Delphi — cast from the weapons of the Persians defeated at Plataea in 479 BC The catch — From mid-morning to dusk this is the hardest-worked square in Turkey: carpet touts, sudden new friends steering you toward a shop, dropped shoe-shine brushes. Come at 07:00 before the coaches, or after dark when it is floodlit and the trade has gone home. Walk like you have an appointment. Sultanahmet, Fatih · Open ground — walkable at any hour, free

old_cards.name: The Obelisk of Theodosius
old_cards.teaser: Already eighteen centuries old when Constantinople put it up.
old_cards.body: The granite was cut for Thutmose III and raised at Karnak, its inscriptions marking his campaign to the Euphrates around 1450 BC. Theodosius I had it shipped from Egypt and re-erected on the spine of the Hippodrome in 390 AD. It lost length in transit, so what stands is the upper section, 18.5 metres of it, on a marble base carved in Constantinople showing the emperor watching the races from his box. Nothing else in the city comes close in age. Sultanahmet Meydanı (At Meydanı) · outdoors, free, at any hour

old_cards.name: Beyazıt Meydanı
old_cards.teaser: The university's square, laid over the biggest forum of Roman Constantinople.
old_cards.body: Under the paving lies the Forum of Theodosius — the Forum Tauri — and around the square stands a full Ottoman-to-Republic ensemble: the Beyazıt II Mosque on one side, the Neo-Renaissance arch of Istanbul University's main gate by the French architect Bourgeois on the other, the Beyazıt Tower rising behind it, and the Beyazıt State Library of 1884 between them — whose renovation turned up the remains of a Byzantine church beneath the floor. The square itself was comprehensively rebuilt and reopened on 6 October 2022, and the redesign worked: it is now the calmest large open space in the old city — students on the steps, seed-sellers and their pigeon clouds, old men on benches under the plane trees on the mosque flank, where the lane dips down to the Sahaflar book market (which has its own card in this guide). What it is for: sitting still in the old city without buying anything. Best in late afternoon, when the light comes low across the mosque courtyard and the university empties. The tell — Tea under the plane trees between the mosque and the book market The catch — The Ordu Caddesi side is a tram-and-traffic hinge, and the square has a long history as the city's protest ground — on demonstration days expect police barriers and skip it. Beyazıt, Fatih · Open ground — walkable at any hour, free

old_cards.name: Ortaköy Meydanı
old_cards.teaser: The one square in the city that sits directly on the Bosphorus, with a Balyan mosque on the quay.
old_cards.body: The Büyük Mecidiye Camii — everyone says Ortaköy Mosque — was built 1854–56 for Sultan Abdülmecid I by Garabet and Nigoğayos Balyan, the Armenian father-and-son architects of Dolmabahçe, and it stands not near the water but on it, ornate European-Baroque stone carving straight out of the strait. A three-year restoration brought it back on 6 June 2014 and it works as a mosque; enter outside prayer times. Behind it, the small square and its lanes run the famous kumpir stalls — the loaded baked potato is Ortaköy's street dish — and café tables to the water's edge. What the square is for: the single frame the city puts on postcards, the 1850s mosque against the first Bosphorus bridge (15 Temmuz Şehitler Köprüsü), and ferries sliding between them. Best on a weekday morning, when you get the quay to yourself and the fishermen; sunset is the photograph but you will share it. The tell — The mosque and the bridge in one look, from the quay rail The catch — Weekend afternoons are shoulder-to-shoulder, and the front-row café tables price the view into the menu. Know the recent history too: in November 2025 a visiting family of four died after a day that ended with Ortaköy kumpir and midye — forensics ultimately traced the deaths to pesticide fumigation at their hotel, not the food, but inspectors sealed several stalls for hygiene in the sweep that followed and the quay stood empty for weeks. The row trades again; pick a busy stall with turnover, and stand at the water. Ortaköy, Beşiktaş · Open ground — walkable at any hour; mosque outside prayer times

old_cards.name: Gülhane Parkı
old_cards.teaser: The outer garden of Topkapı Palace, and the city's oldest public park.
old_cards.body: This was the wooded outer garden of Topkapı, opened to the public by the municipality in 1912 — the oldest public park in Istanbul, just under ten hectares falling from the palace walls toward Sarayburnu, where the Bosphorus meets the Marmara. Its name is in the history books: the Tanzimat edict, the decree that began the empire's modernisation, was read at Gülhane on 3 November 1839. The renovations of the 2000s stripped out the old zoo and funfair, and what is left is the right thing — lawns, very old planes with grey herons in them, and the Goths Column, a Roman victory monument, standing near the lower end. On the park's edges sit the Alay Köşkü on the outer wall and the Islamic science and technology museum in the former palace stables; the Archaeological Museums (which have their own card) are entered from here too. What it is for: the only place to feel the palace's ground without a ticket, and the shortest escape from Sultanahmet's crowds — two minutes from the tram. The tell — The walk downhill under the planes to the Goths Column and the sea The catch — A public city park with gates — go in daylight; we did not verify posted closing times. Know that the municipality shuts its parks outright on severe-storm alerts (Gülhane was closed for one in August 2025) — on an orange-warning day, don't bother. Gülhane, Fatih — below Topkapı

old_cards.name: Emirgan Korusu
old_cards.tag: Khedive's grove · tulips in April · free
old_cards.teaser: A khedive's exile estate above the Bosphorus — and in April, the densest flowerbed in Turkey.
old_cards.body: Forty-seven hectares of grove above the Emirgan shore, once the estate of Khedive İsmail Paşa of Egypt, who lived out his exile here; the city took it over in the 1940s and the İBB runs it now. His three 19th-century pavilions survive, restored 1979–83 — the Sarı Köşk (the yellow one, the park's centrepiece, run as a café by the municipal operator Beltur since 1997), the Beyaz Köşk and the Pembe Köşk, all trading as municipal cafés and function rooms. The tulip reality: since 2005 the April tulip festival has made Emirgan its main stage, millions of bulbs in set-piece beds — it is genuinely spectacular and genuinely mobbed, with the shore road jammed on festival weekends. Any other month you get one of the great groves of the city nearly to yourself: steep paths, ponds, huge pines, and the Bosphorus flashing between trunks. Pairs naturally with the Sakıp Sabancı Museum at the bottom of the hill (see the crafts pages). The tell — The Sarı Köşk seen across the pond, out of tulip season, in silence The catch — April means crowds and parking misery — come by bus or ferry-plus-walk. Pavilion café hours unverified; the grove itself is the point. Emirgan, Sarıyer

old_cards.name: Fethi Paşa Korusu
old_cards.tag: Asian-side grove · the bridge view · free
old_cards.teaser: The Asian shore's vizier's grove, with the first bridge filling the whole view.
old_cards.body: Some thirteen hectares of wooded hillside dropping to the Bosphorus just north of Üsküdar, named for Fethi Ahmed Paşa, the Ottoman vizier whose estate this was. After decades of neglect it was renewed and opened fully to the public, and it is now the local answer to the European shore's manicured parks — steeper, quieter, and pointed straight at the water: the terraces look across at Ortaköy and the European towers with the first Bosphorus bridge overhead, close enough to read the traffic. A municipal social facility — the Fethipaşa Sosyal Tesisi — trades inside the grove with tea and breakfast. What it is for: the postcard panorama without a single tour group. This is where Üsküdar families do Sunday breakfast; a visitor here has left the circuit entirely. Walk in from Kuzguncuk's one street (which has its own card) and the morning makes itself. The tell — Breakfast-hour view of the bridge from the upper terrace The catch — Paths are steep and shade is real — flat shoes. Facility hours unverified; the terraces and the view are free and always there. Paşalimanı, Üsküdar — between Kuzguncuk and Sultantepe

old_cards.name: Büyük Valide Han
old_cards.teaser: The largest caravanserai in the city, still working — and no, you cannot go on the roof.
old_cards.body: Kösem Sultan — mother of two sultans, and for a stretch the most powerful woman in Ottoman history — built this around 1651 to fund her Çinili complex: 210 rooms around three courtyards, the largest historic han in Istanbul. It was the base of the city's Iranian merchant colony, whose small Shia mescit still stands in the courtyard; grand Muharram ceremonies were held here until 1927, when such processions were banned. It is severely dilapidated — the third courtyard is largely ruinous, with a Byzantine tower, the Tower of Eirene, standing at its corner — but it is not a ruin: a handful of foundry and mould-making workshops still trade in the galleries (most of the old textile ateliers have given way to wholesalers' storage), and that is the thing to see, a 17th-century building doing its original job. Now the truth the Instagram captions omit: the famous rooftop, with its dome-field view to the Golden Horn, was officially closed by the Culture and Tourism Ministry in 2016 after visitor traffic damaged the domes — warning signs are posted. Anyone offering to take you up for a banknote is selling you a violation of a closure order on a fragile roof. Go at working hours, walk the courtyards, and remember it is somebody's workplace. The tell — The main courtyard: workshops, the Iranian mescit, and the Byzantine tower behind The catch — Roof access banned since 2016 — we found no evidence of any legal reopening as of August 2026, and a fire broke out on that same roof in June 2026, so the fabric is more fragile than ever; check access on the day. Courtyards only, weekday working hours, and mind the crumbling stone. Mercan, Fatih — above the Grand Bazaar

old_cards.name: Rüstem Paşa Camii
old_cards.teaser: Sinan's tile box, hidden on a terrace above the market that pays for it.
old_cards.body: You will walk past it unless you know: the mosque sits on a raised terrace above a block of vaulted shops in Tahtakale, and the way in is an easy-to-miss stair off the market street. The shops are not an accident — their rents endowed the mosque, commerce below, prayer above, which is the whole Ottoman city in one section drawing. Sinan finished it around 1563 for Rüstem Paşa, Süleyman's grand vizier and husband of Mihrimah Sultan, a man repairing his reputation with beauty. What makes it singular: some 2,300 İznik tiles in roughly eighty patterns cover the interior — no other mosque anywhere makes such lavish use of them — including the tomato-red Armenian bole, the pigment İznik's kilns mastered for a few decades in the 16th century and then lost forever. The red near the qibla wall is the colour ceramicists still cannot fully reproduce. Closed for years of restoration, it reopened for worship in 2021. Free; go between prayer times, dress covered, and give your eyes ten minutes to adjust. The tell — The lost İznik tomato-red on the qibla wall The catch — A working mosque — closed to visits during the five daily prayers, and shoulders and knees covered. Tahtakale, Eminönü — beside the Spice Bazaar · Working mosque — visit outside prayer times, free

old_cards.name: Küçük Ayasofya Camii
old_cards.teaser: Justinian's other Hagia Sophia — older ground, no queue, no ticket.
old_cards.body: Ten minutes downhill from the Sultanahmet queues stands the church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, begun by Justinian early in his reign — scholars put it between 527 and 536, some arguing for the mid-520s, contemporary with the great Hagia Sophia and possibly earlier. It is the oldest surviving Justinianic church building in the city that you can simply walk into. The proof is carved into the building: around the interior runs the original Greek inscription frieze naming the emperor Justinian and the empress Theodora — and, in a small act of sixth-century editing, mentioning Saint Sergius while leaving Saint Bacchus out. It became a mosque between 1506 and 1513 under Hüseyin Ağa, chief eunuch of the palace, was restored through 2006, and now works as a quiet neighbourhood mosque: octagon under a dome, whitewash and carved marble, carpet underfoot, mostly empty outside prayer times. What it is for: standing alone inside a sixth-century imperial building while the crowds queue up the hill. The tell — The marble frieze that still names Justinian and Theodora The catch — A working mosque — outside prayer times, shoes off, covered shoulders. The name on maps is Küçük Ayasofya Camii. Küçük Ayasofya, Fatih — below the Hippodrome · Working mosque — visit outside prayer times, free

x-ebristan.angle_note: the craft (UNESCO 2014) and the master; verify how to enrol: if no open enrolment can be confirmed, say 'by arrangement' honestly

old_cards.name: Ebristan — Hikmet Barutçugil
old_cards.teaser: The marbler who invented his own pattern and named it gunpowder.
old_cards.body: Hikmet Barutçugil, born in Malatya in 1952, trained as a textile designer at the Istanbul State Academy of Fine Arts and turned to marbling in 1977. He opened Ebristan in Salacak, on the Üsküdar shore, in 1996, and works ebru onto cloth, ceramic, glass, wood and wax as well as paper. One pattern carries his name — barut ebrusu, gunpowder marbling. He teaches constantly; sessions are arranged directly rather than booked through a platform. Salacak, Üsküdar — the Asian shore facing the old city

old_cards.name: Ebru — marbling
old_cards.teaser: Colour floated on thickened water and lifted onto paper in a single breath.
old_cards.body: Pigment ground from earth and mineral, cut with ox gall so it floats, dropped onto water thickened with tragacanth, combed into flowers and stones and waves, then lifted off in one sheet. UNESCO inscribed it in 2014. It was never decorative on its own terms: ebru was made for bookbinders, as endpapers, and as a ground for official documents that could not be forged twice. It lived inside the book trade, not beside it. Practised across the city; taught in Üsküdar and in Sultanahmet

x-caferaga.group: The others, and what each is missing
x-caferaga.angle_note: courses in Sinan's medrese: what is missing (e.g. no master named publicly)

old_cards.name: Caferağa Medresesi
old_cards.teaser: Sinan's medrese behind Hagia Sophia, still teaching the crafts in its cells.
old_cards.body: Mimar Sinan built this medrese for Cafer Ağa in 1559, in the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent, immediately behind Hagia Sophia. Since 1989 the Türk Kültürüne Hizmet Vakfı has run it as a working crafts school: ebru, hüsn-i hat, tezhip gilding, çini and ceramic, miniature, stained glass, jewellery, felt and weaving, taught in the old student cells around the courtyard. Full courses run over months; shorter sessions exist for visitors. Ask at the gate. Caferiye Sok., Sultanahmet, Fatih — immediately behind Hagia Sophia

x-cini.group: The others, and what each is missing
x-cini.angle_note: the craft; where to see and what is missing for a visitor who wants to learn

old_cards.name: Çini — the İznik blue
old_cards.teaser: A Turkish word that means Chinese, and it is being honest.
old_cards.body: Çini is Çin — China — with an ending: Ottoman potters were chasing the prestige of imported Chinese blue-and-white, and the language kept the receipt. The İznik body is the trick, up to eighty-five per cent quartz, which is why the glaze reads as lit from behind. Production stopped in the seventeenth century and took the recipe with it. The İznik Foundation, founded in 1993 by the economist Işıl Akbaygil, reverse-engineered the quartz body and fired again from 1995. Made in İznik, Bursa province; sold and taught in Istanbul

x-hat.group: The others, and what each is missing
x-hat.angle_note: the craft, and the Sabancı collection as where to see it

old_cards.name: Hüsn-i hat — calligraphy
old_cards.teaser: Writing measured in dots, where the shape of the letter is the point.
old_cards.body: Arabic-script calligraphy written to proportion: every letter measured in rhombic dots laid down by the same reed pen, so a hand is judged on its geometry before its content. The kit is fixed — reed pen, trimming slab, soot ink, paper sized and burnished until the ink cannot bleed. UNESCO inscribed it in 2021. Istanbul is where the Ottoman masters set the proportions the rest of the Islamic world then copied, teacher to pupil, by licence. Best seen at the Sakıp Sabancı Museum, Emirgan

old_cards.name: Sakıp Sabancı Museum — the book arts
old_cards.teaser: Five hundred years of Ottoman hands, inside a 1927 villa on the Bosphorus.
old_cards.body: The Atlı Köşk at Emirgan, built in 1927 by the Italian architect Edouard De Nari, holds what Sakıp Sabancı spent a lifetime buying: five centuries of Ottoman book arts — manuscript Qur'ans, calligraphic panels, albums, hilyes, imperial documents. It began with a single panel by Sultan Mahmud II. The family handed the house and the collection to Sabancı University in 1998 on a forty-nine-year lease, and the museum opened in 2002. This is where hüsn-i hat stops being a description. Emirgan, Sarıyer — on the European Bosphorus shore, north of Beşiktaş

old_cards.name: Carpets and "antiques" — the honest note
old_cards.teaser: If it is genuinely antique, you are not allowed to take it home.
old_cards.body: Turkish law protects cultural property, and genuinely old carpets, tiles, coins and icons cannot legally leave the country; dealers selling older pieces are expected to hand over museum certification that an item is not an antiquity. Which tells you precisely what the "three-hundred-year-old" rug on the wall is. A reputable seller produces that paperwork unprompted. And turn any rug over — hand-knotted backs are slightly irregular, machine-made ones suspiciously perfect. Applies anywhere in Turkey, not only inside the bazaar

a-grand-bazaar.angle_note: the bazaar and its gold street in one card

old_cards.name: Kapalıçarşı — the Grand Bazaar
old_cards.teaser: Sixty-one streets named for guilds that mostly no longer trade on them.
old_cards.body: Mehmed II began it within three years of the conquest; its stone bedesten for cloth and gems was finished by 1461, and it grew into sixty-one covered streets and more than four thousand shops across 30,700 square metres. Every lane was a guild, and the street names are the surviving record of trades that have since left them: the main artery, Kalpakçılar Caddesi, is Hatmakers' Street, and has not sold a fur hat in living memory. It is now solid gold, end to end. Fatih · roughly Mon–Sat 09:00–19:00 · closed Sundays and religious holidays

old_cards.name: Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the gold
old_cards.teaser: Turks buy gold the way other countries buy government bonds.
old_cards.body: This is the part of the bazaar that is not theatre. Turkish households have held savings in gold for decades because the lira keeps losing value, so the jewellers here are serving locals as much as visitors, and the price is arithmetic rather than performance: the day's gram rate, plus a workmanship charge. Ask for those two numbers separately. The conversation stops being a haggle and becomes a discussion about who made the piece. Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the bazaar's main axis, Beyazıt gate to Nuruosmaniye gate

old_cards.name: Zincirli Han
old_cards.teaser: The courtyard where the hammering is real and nobody chases you.
old_cards.body: Built in 1708 on the caravanserai plan — shops below, workshops and lodgings above — and historically the han for goldsmithing and jewellery, with carpet and antique dealers alongside. It is the quietest courtyard in the bazaar and still the most working one: metal is melted and copper hammered behind the shopfronts, by ateliers that have run for generations. The master-and-apprentice chain has thinned badly. It has not broken. Go on a weekday morning and stand still. Northern end of the Grand Bazaar, Fatih · bazaar hours

old_cards.name: Sahaflar Çarşısı
old_cards.teaser: A book market on Byzantine ground, now mostly selling exam crammers.
old_cards.body: The booksellers' courtyard between the Grand Bazaar and Beyazıt Mosque stands on the Chartoprateia, the Byzantine paper and book market — the trade has not moved in a thousand years. Sahaf is Arabic: a dealer in written sheets. Ottoman booksellers left the Grand Bazaar for this yard in the eighteenth century; fire took it in the 1950s and it was rebuilt. Honest now — computers and then the internet hollowed the antiquarian trade out, and much of the stock is exam crammers. Between the Grand Bazaar and Beyazıt Mosque, Fatih · daily, daylight hours

a-galip-dede.group: The music street — instruments and vinyl

old_cards.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
old_cards.name: Galip Dede Caddesi — the music street
old_cards.teaser: The whole instrument trade on one downhill street, the good beside the useless.
old_cards.body: The street falls from Tünel to the Galata Tower and has been the musicians' bazaar for decades: darbuka, davul and frame drums, bağlama and saz, ney and zurna, plus string sellers and repair benches behind the counters. The honest warning is unavoidable — a large share of the bağlamas in the windows are decorative and close to unplayable. Ask to hear one played before you think about buying. If nobody in the shop can play it, that is your answer. Galip Dede Cad., Beyoğlu — Tünel down to the Galata Tower · daytime

old_cards.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
old_cards.name: Saz, bağlama, kanun, ud — what the names admit
old_cards.teaser: Four instrument names, four different empires answering at once.
old_cards.body: Saz is simply Persian for "instrument". Bağlama comes from bağlamak, to tie, after the gut frets tied round the neck and slid by hand — which is why the thing plays intervals a piano cannot. Kanun is Greek, kanōn, a rule or measuring rod, because the zither lays down the law of pitch that the singer and the rest of the ensemble tune to. Ud is Arabic al-ʿūd, the wood, and it is where our word lute comes from.

a-manol.group: The music street — instruments and vinyl

old_cards.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
old_cards.name: Manol, and who actually built the oud
old_cards.teaser: The Turkish oud has an inventor, and his name was Manol.
old_cards.body: The Metropolitan Museum, which owns one of his instruments, records Emmanuel Venios — Manol — as Greek, born on Folegandros about 1838 and dead in Istanbul in 1915 or 1916; he had a workshop on İstiklal by about 1870. He is credited with the smaller, higher-tuned instrument the world now calls the Turkish oud, and his are still held to be the finest ever built. The other great maker of the tradition, Onnik Karibyan, working a generation later, was Armenian. The instrument at the centre of Turkish classical music was designed and refined by the communities this city lost. A lineage, not an address — the living trade is on Galip Dede Caddesi, Beyoğlu

a-lale-plak.group: The music street — instruments and vinyl

old_cards.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
old_cards.name: Lale Plak
old_cards.teaser: Half a century at the top of the music street, run by one ear.
old_cards.body: At the Tünel end of the music street, and among the oldest record shops in the city — trading for well over fifty years, with the exact founding year disputed between sources. Hakan Atala's stock runs from Western classical and jazz, signed pressings included, to the 1970s Turkish canon: Barış Manço, Ajda Pekkan, the Anadolu rock era. It is a shop to be served in rather than to browse. Say what you are after and let him pull it. Galip Dede Cad., Tünel, Beyoğlu
